title: 3D Printing
objective: After this level you can explain how 3D printers build objects layer by layer.
summary: 3D printing builds objects layer upon layer instead of cutting away. Hull's 1983 stereolithography used UV light; Crump's glue-gun frog led to FDM in 1989.

cards.headline: In 1988, a father tried to make his daughter a toy frog with a glue gun.
cards.body: Scott Crump loaded the gun with a mix of polyethylene and candle wax and built the frog up layer by layer. Then he wondered how a machine could do the same. His answer turned into one kind of 3D printer.

cards.headline: Adding, not cutting
cards.body: Most making is subtractive: you drill, cut or mill material away until the part is left, like a sculptor with a block. A 3D printer is additive. It takes a digital 3D model and builds the object layer upon layer. Nothing is carved away, which is why 3D printers are widely used to make complex components in all sorts of materials.

events.label: Chuck Hull develops stereolithography: UV light hardens liquid polymer, layer by layer
Hull's patent is issued; he co-founds 3D Systems
The SLA-1, the first 3D printer made for commercial sale
Crump patents fused deposition modeling: melted plastic from a moving head
Stratasys produces the first FDM machine

cards.fact: 3D printing shines at prototypes and things made for one person.
cards.context: It is a leading technology for rapid prototyping, and it makes custom, patient-specific items such as hearing aids, dental aligners, implants and prosthetics. That is the opposite of Level 87's line, which turned out more than 15 million Model Ts. Mass production makes many of the same thing; a 3D printer shines when each one is different.

mascot.line: Level 87's line, turned around: millions of copies of one design, or one copy of each.

cards.headline: 3D printing: layered
learned: Additive: build layer upon layer instead of cutting away
Hull, 1983: stereolithography with UV light; SLA-1 sold in 1987
Crump's glue-gun frog led to melted-plastic FDM in 1989
Best at prototypes and one-person custom parts

options.label: It cuts material away from a solid block
It builds the object layer upon layer
It adds paint after the part is carved
options.rationale: Additive means adding material layer by layer.

options.label: It glues finished parts together
options.rationale: It builds the part itself, layer by layer.

questions.explanation: A 3D printer builds an object layer upon layer from a digital model instead of removing material.

questions.prompt: In Chuck Hull's stereolithography, what turns liquid into each solid layer?

options.label: A glue gun of melted wax
Hot air drying the liquid out
options.rationale: It is hardened by light, not dried.

options.label: Ultraviolet light hardening a liquid polymer
A drill carving a solid block

questions.explanation: Stereolithography uses ultraviolet light to harden liquid photopolymer one layer at a time.

questions.prompt: At Lomekwi (Level 1), someone made the oldest known tools by knocking flakes off stones. What kind of making is that?

options.label: Additive: building up layer by layer
options.rationale: That's 3D printing; flaking stone takes material away.

options.label: Mass production on a moving line
options.rationale: That's Ford's line, over 3 million years later.

questions.explanation: Knocking off flakes removes material until the tool is left, the opposite of a 3D printer's additive layers.
